name: Monads
summary: A wrapper type plus one rule for chaining steps, so the plumbing (missing values, errors, waiting, state) is written once instead of after every step.
howItWorks: Many steps return more than a plain value: maybe nothing (`Option`), a value or an error (`Result`), a value later (a future), or several values (a list). Chaining such steps by hand means writing the same check after each one: is it null, did it fail, has it arrived? A monad moves that check into the type. It needs two operations. One wraps a plain value (`Some(x)`, `Ok(x)`, Haskell’s `return`). The other chains: given a wrapped value and a function from a plain value to a new wrapped value, it returns the next wrapped value. It is called `bind` or `>>=` in Haskell, `flatMap` in Java and JavaScript, `and_then` in Rust, `SelectMany` in C#. The chaining function is where the plumbing lives, written once: for `Option` it stops at the first empty step, for `Result` at the first error, for a list it runs the next step on every element and flattens the results. Three laws say that wrapping a value adds nothing and that it doesn’t matter how you group a chain, so steps can be refactored freely. Languages add sugar so chains read like ordinary code: Haskell’s `do` blocks, Rust’s `?`, C#’s query syntax. The name comes from category theory, but you can use one without knowing any.
analogy: An assembly line with a reject chute. Each station does its job on the part; a part that fails a check drops into the chute, and the stations after it never see it. The chute is built into the conveyor once, not into every station.
useWhen: Chains of steps where any step can fail or come back empty: parsing, validation, lookups
Replacing nested null checks or try/catch blocks with one straight chain
Libraries for async work, parsers or state, where one combinator (`flatMap`) works across many types
avoidWhen: Languages without the sugar, where hand-written `flatMap` pyramids read worse than early returns
Teaching a team through category theory; start from `Option` and `Result`
Generic code that assumes every `then` or `flatMap` obeys the laws; JavaScript promises don’t
example: Signing up a user takes three steps that can each fail: read the email from the request body, validate it, and insert it into the database, which refuses a duplicate. Each step returns `Ok(value)` or `Err(reason)`. In Rust each call ends with `?`, so the first `Err` returns from the function and later steps never run, and no error check is written between the lines. `signup("email=nope")` returns `Err(BadEmail)` without touching the database.

source: // `?` unwraps an Ok, or returns the Err from signup right away
// the same chain written with and_then, the flatMap of Result
println!("{:?}", signup("email=nope"));              // Err(BadEmail): insert never ran

sections.title: The laws, and why a Promise is only nearly a monad
body: Haskell’s standard library states three laws. Left identity: wrapping a value and chaining a function is the same as calling the function (`return a >>= k` equals `k a`). Right identity: chaining the wrap function changes nothing. Associativity: chaining `f` then `g` is the same as chaining one function that does `f` then `g`. Together they mean you can extract or inline steps of a chain without changing what it does. Haskell does not check them; it trusts each type’s author.

JavaScript’s `then` behaves like both `map` and `flatMap`: if your callback returns a promise, or any object with a `then` method, the Promises/A+ resolution procedure adopts it instead of wrapping it. That is convenient (you never see a promise of a promise) but it breaks left identity. If `x` is an object with a `then` method, `Promise.resolve(x).then(f)` hands `f` whatever `x` resolves to, while `f(x)` gets `x` itself. In April 2013 a request to give the spec a strictly monadic interface was closed without being adopted. For everyday code this rarely matters; for libraries that treat all monads alike, it does.

sections.title: Build one in TypeScript
sections.intro: A tiny `Result` with a `flatMap`. The check for failure is written once, in `flatMap`, and every step after a failure is skipped.
source: type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
const ok = <T>(value: T): Result<T, never> => ({ ok: true, value });
const err = <E>(error: E): Result<never, E> => ({ ok: false, error });
// the whole trick: the "did it fail?" check is written once, here
const flatMap = <T, U, E>(r: Result<T, E>, f: (t: T) => Result<U, E>): Result<U, E> =>
console.log(flatMap(parseAge("x"), adult));  // { ok: false, error: "not a number" }: adult never ran

story: Monads came into computing from semantics, not from programming practice. In 1989, at the LICS conference, Eugenio Moggi showed how monads from category theory could describe features of programming languages such as state and exceptions in one uniform way; the full version, “Notions of computation and monads”, appeared in 1991. His goal was a correct basis for proving programs equivalent across many “notions of computation”.

Philip Wadler saw that the same structure could organise ordinary functional programs. In “The essence of functional programming” (POPL 1992) and “Comprehending monads”, he used monads to hide the plumbing: a counter, error handling or other state threaded through a computation without being passed by hand at every call. This mattered to Haskell, a pure, lazy language whose input and output were awkward: Haskell 1.0 (1990) described I/O as streams of requests and responses, or as continuations. Simon Peyton Jones and Wadler’s “Imperative functional programming” (1993) showed monadic I/O working, and the Haskell 1.3 report of May 1996 adopted it, together with `do` notation.

Haskell’s `Monad` type class turned the idea into reusable code: functions like `sequence` are written once and work for every monad. From there the pattern spread under friendlier names. Java 8 (2014) shipped `Optional.flatMap`, C#’s LINQ query syntax translates nested `from` clauses into `SelectMany`, and Rust’s `Option` and `Result` offer `and_then` and the `?` operator. JavaScript went the other way: in 2013 the Promises/A+ community discussed and declined a strictly monadic design, keeping a `then` that unwraps anything promise-like.

choices.choice: Borrow a structure from category theory
choices.why: Moggi wanted one modular way to describe many notions of computation (state, exceptions, nondeterminism) instead of building a special semantics for each feature.
With a `Monad` class, combinators like `sequence` are written once and work for every monad. Intellectual reuse became code reuse, and the need drove extensions to Haskell’s type classes.

choices.choice: I/O as a value that describes an action
choices.why: A value of type `IO a` is a computation that, when performed, may do input and output and then deliver an `a`. That kept Haskell pure while giving it ordinary-looking I/O, replacing the stream and continuation designs.
The compiler cannot verify the three laws, so Haskell trusts each instance’s author. In practice some types are used monadically even where the laws don’t hold.
